heroHeadline: Trump-Brokered 3-Day Ukraine–Russia Ceasefire Takes Effect on Victory Day — Lebanon Ceasefire Collapses Further (13+ Killed May 8); ASEAN Summit Concludes With No Myanmar Breakthrough
heroSubtitle: On May 9, 2026 — Russia's Victory Day — a U.S.-brokered 3-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine took effect, with both Presidents Putin and Zelensky accepting the truce window running through May 11. Russia held a scaled-down Victory Day parade without heavy military hardware on display for the first time in nearly two decades — reflecting both the war's toll on materiel and the diplomatic sensitivity of the moment. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff brokered the arrangement after two competing unilateral ceasefire bids earlier in the week collapsed immediately (Russia's own Victory Day truce and Ukraine's counter-proposal both failed within hours, with Russia launching 108 drones and 3 missiles and Zelensky reporting 1,820 violations). The 3-day ceasefire is the first mutually accepted ceasefire window since Russia's February 24, 2022 full invasion — a significant symbolic milestone, though underlying peace negotiations remain stalled over control of Donetsk, NATO membership, and security guarantees. On May 8, Lebanon's ceasefire suffered its deadliest single day since being declared April 17: Israeli strikes killed at least 13 people in south Lebanon, continuing the pattern of systematic Israeli military operations despite the nominal three-week extension running to ~May 14. Lebanon filed a fresh UN Security Council complaint. A second round of Lebanon-Israel direct talks was scheduled for Washington on May 14–15 — a diplomatic pathway forward even as the ceasefire continues to collapse in practice. The 48th ASEAN Summit concluded in Cebu on May 9 with only 'tiny shifts' on Myanmar: five years after the Five-Point Consensus was adopted, ASEAN foreign ministers agreed only to schedule a virtual meeting with Myanmar's foreign minister, producing no enforcement mechanisms. The US-Iran MOU framework process continued through Pakistan's back-channel, with Iran's formal response to the one-page MOU expected by May 8 — reports suggest Tehran described the US text as 'more of an American wish list than a reality' and continued to insist on enrichment rights and UN Security Council-backed guarantees.
footerNote: Data sourced from UN, African Union, IGAD, Crisis Group, USIP, PA-X Database, and Tier 1–3 sources across all media poles.
